title: Bangladeshi Cleaners Executed in Saudi Arabia After Families Were Not Told of Death Sentences
excerpt: Sweety Akhtar and Nazrul Islam, cleaners from Bangladesh, were executed in Makkah on October 14. A prisoner list sent to the Bangladesh consulate two weeks earlier did not mention death sentences, and their families learned of the executions from the news.
body:
• Sweety Akhtar and Nazrul Islam, Bangladeshi cleaners working in Saudi Arabia, were executed in the Makkah region on October 14, 2026.
  • Saudi Arabia's Interior Ministry said they were convicted of an 'immoral act' inside a mosque; a Saudi prisoner list had recorded different allegations — adultery against Akhtar and a cybercrime offence against Islam.
  • The Bangladesh Consulate General in Jeddah received that list, naming 97 prisoners, on September 30. The death-sentence column was blank, and Bangladeshi officials did not follow up, according to foreign ministry sources.
  • Neither family knew a death sentence existed. Akhtar spoke to her father on October 13 and said she might be released within two months; she was executed the next day.

Sweety Akhtar last spoke to her father on October 13. Calling from a Saudi prison, she said nothing about a death sentence and had earlier told her family she might be released within two months. The next day, Saudi Arabia executed her.

Nazrul Islam's family was blindsided in the same way. The 22-year-old cleaner spoke to them from prison on Sundays. More than three years after his arrest, they learned from the media that he had been executed on October 14, according to The Business Standard.

Two Workers, One Employer

Akhtar was the youngest of five daughters of Fazal Mia, a day labourer in Mirzapur, Tangail. Her father borrowed Tk 1.5 lakh to send her to Saudi Arabia, where she arrived in late 2022 and worked as a cleaner for a company called Al Majal. She was divorced, and her young daughter has been raised by her elder sister since she left, The Daily Star reported. Islam's father borrowed Tk 7 lakh to send his son abroad in November 2022; he worked as a cleaner for the same company.

Islam was detained on August 1, 2023 under Saudi Arabia's cybercrime law. Akhtar was detained the next day over an allegation of adultery, according to a memo the Bangladesh Consulate General in Jeddah sent to Dhaka on October 18. The Saudi Interior Ministry later said both were convicted of an "immoral act" inside a mosque in Makkah. The consulate's letter does not reconcile those two accounts, and it does not establish whether either defendant had legal representation or an interpreter of their choosing.

The List That Said Nothing

On September 30 — two weeks before the executions — Saudi authorities shared a routine list of 97 Bangladeshi prisoners with the Jeddah consulate. It named Islam and Akhtar and their alleged offences, but the column for death sentences was blank. Foreign ministry sources told the Times of Bangladesh that mission officials made no effort to contact Saudi authorities about the cases, despite a labour wing of more than 100 staff whose work includes legal assistance to detained workers.

"If engaged with the Saudi authorities without any delay, their capital punishment could have been deferred or judgement might be altered."

— A former Bangladeshi diplomat who served in the Middle East, to the Times of Bangladesh

One official conceded the mission had been told the offences but not the punishment. Another, who had served in the kingdom, said labour-wing officials know such charges can carry the death penalty in Saudi Arabia — which made the absence of any inquiry harder to explain.

What Dhaka Is Seeking Now

Bangladesh was not notified of the death sentences or the executions in advance and is now seeking the judgments, details of the proceedings, and answers on whether the two received a meaningful opportunity to defend themselves. Akhtar's family learned of her death around October 18, four days after the execution, through other people. As of October 20, her father said the government had not contacted the family.

"Whether she is alive or dead, I just want my daughter back," her mother, Johura, told The Daily Star. Islam's father is asking for his son's body while creditors demand repayment of the loan that sent him to Saudi Arabia.

For the millions of South Asian families with a member working in the Gulf, the case turns on a practical failure: the information needed to intervene existed, in Dhaka's own consulate, two weeks before the executions — and no system acted on it.
